item.title: Can the Men in Your Life Talk to You About Sexual Assault?
item.description:
Sexual Abuse

Can the Men in Your Life Talk to You About Sexual Assault?

How we can dismantle barriers to care for men who experience sexual trauma.

Posted August 15, 2026

Key points
  • Many men who experience sexual trauma wait decades—on average, 15-20 years—to tell anyone.
  • Buying into male rape myths can block supportive disclosure.
  • Hegemonic masculinity expectations uniquely silences male survivors.
  • You can become a person that is safe to disclose to.

Imagine learning that someone you care about—a partner, friend, or brother—has carried a story of sexual assault for decades and never told a soul—not even you.

For 16 years, I have worked as a psychologist at a large VA hospital (as well as in a small private practice), sitting with hundreds of men who have experienced unwanted sexual contact. In these rooms, behind closed doors, stories surface that many had kept hidden for decades.

Over and over, I have witnessed relief and integration begin the moment a man finds permission to share his experience with someone who listens without judgment. The most common regret I hear is, “I wish I would have talked about this sooner.”

And yet, many men struggle to find a safe space for disclosure. During the #MeToo movement, several men I worked with shared that they felt invisible within the broader conversation—and, at times, even perceived as potential perpetrators rather than survivors.

It’s time to rethink and reshape the narrative.

The Myths That Keep Men Silent

We are surrounded by beliefs that make it harder for men to talk about sexual violence. Are you a safe person for disclosure? Check yourself against these common myths from the Male Rape Myth Scale, Shortened Version (MRMS-SV, Weare & Willmott, 2026).

  • Women who rape men are sexually frustrated individuals.
  • The extent of a man’s resistance should be a major factor in determining whether he was raped.
  • I would have a hard time believing a man who told me that he was raped by a woman.
  • Male rape is usually committed by homosexuals.
  • A man can enjoy sex even if it is being forced upon him.
  • Most men who are raped by a woman are somewhat to blame for not escaping or fighting off the woman.
  • Many men claim rape if they have consented to homosexual relations but have changed their minds afterward.
  • Any healthy man can successfully resist a rapist if he really wants to.
  • If a man obtained an erection while being raped, it probably means that he started to enjoy it.
  • Most men who are raped by a woman are somewhat to blame for not being more careful.
  • If a man engages in necking and petting and he lets things get out of hand, it is his own fault if his partner forces sex on him.
  • No self-respecting man would admit to being raped.
  • If a man told me that he had been raped by another man, I would suspect that he is homosexual.
  • Men who parade around nude in a locker room are asking for trouble.
  • A man who has been raped has lost his manhood.
  • Male rape is more serious when the victim is heterosexual than when the victim is homosexual.
  • Most men who have been raped have a history of promiscuity.
  • Most men who are raped by a man are somewhat to blame for not escaping or fighting off the man.
  • A man who allows himself to be raped by another man is probably homosexual.
article continues after advertisement

These are cultural myths we may have absorbed. The question is not whether you have had these thoughts, but whether you buy into them, and what you do next. Will you challenge them, seek out more stories, and become a more compassionate witness?

Barriers to Disclosure: What Keeps Men Silent?

Statistically, you probably know many men who have experienced sexual assault. The Center for Disease Control (2024) reports that nearly one in four men in the U.S. have endured some form of contact sexual violence.

Yet men wait far longer to disclose, are less likely to report, and have fewer places to turn for safety than women (Langdridge et al., 2023; Pilkington et al., 2026). Disclosure can be delayed for decades—on average, from 15-20 years. Why?

“Hegemonic masculinity” norms set the rules: Never show fear, sadness, or vulnerability; always remain dominant, self-reliant, and in control. Sexual victimization collides directly with these norms.

After an assault, men often minimize what happened, blame themselves (“I should have fought back”), question their sexuality, or struggle with shame, anxiety, and anger. Many isolate or use substances, feeling they have no cultural “place” as victims—especially if the perpetrator is a woman, or if they are men of color or from cultures with especially restrictive gender roles.

Societal responses often compound the pain. Disclosure may be met with disbelief, minimization, or hostile questioning (“Are you gay?” “Why didn’t you stop it?”), and men fear being labeled as weak, aggressive, or dangerous themselves (Pilkington et al., 2026).

Institutional reactions often worsen the problem. Survivors report fearing they will not be believed or, worse, will be blamed—by police, providers, family, even friends. Institutional betrayal (McAdams et al., 2025) like having military leadership dismiss a disclosure, can feel even more damaging than the trauma itself, leading to avoidance, worsened PTSD, and mistrust of help. Men have been labeled as "weak" or "broken," made fun of, or punished (Pilkington et al., 2026).

article continues after advertisement

How We Can Help: Moving Toward Integration and Support

Men who have been able to disclose and receive supportive, validating responses often experience relief, decreased shame, and improved quality of life. Research indicates that asking about sexual trauma directly, inviting stories with openness, and helping men find community with other survivors are transformative (Pilkington et al., 2026).

Men who have spoken publicly about their experiences of sexual trauma and recovery have created pathways for others to seek support. For example, in a 2019 article in the New York Times (Phillipps, 2019), six individuals shared their stories of military sexual trauma (MST), bringing much-needed visibility to this issue. Others have come forward through platforms like About Face and Make the Connection. With estimates indicating that as many men as women experience MST—at least 10,000 annually—the willingness of these men to tell their stories has led to improved care and greater recognition of the unique needs of male veterans.

Steps to Take to Better Support Male Survivors

If you want to support men in your life:

  • Educate yourself about male sexual trauma—start by challenging myths and assumptions.
  • Listen with compassion.
  • Offer to help connect them with resources.
  • Advocate for better training and cultural change in institutions serving men.

If you are a man who has experienced sexual assault and are considering disclosure:

  • Hear from men who have experienced sexual trauma and have found recovery.
  • Find a therapist who understands male sexual trauma and is certified in evidence-based PTSD treatment.
  • Find a survivor group through an advocacy group like RAINN (Rape, Abuse, and Incest National Network) or MaleSurvivor.

To find mental health support near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Are You Launching a College Freshman?
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Are You Launching a College Freshman?

Ideas for embracing the milestone transition between high school and college.

Posted August 15, 2026

Key points
  • Kids going off to college means a wave of transition for students and families.
  • When students launch, it can feel like the family is shrinking; in reality, it's a time of incredible growth.
  • Families often focus on how much to communicate instead of focusing on the quality of communication.
  • The healthiest families stay deeply connected while giving one another room to grow.

It’s back-to-school season and for college freshman, that means a wave of transition for students and families. It was a a genuine pleasure to discuss the important family dynamics of the college launch with our local television program Good Day DC, and I thought I would share some of the thoughts from our conversation.

Managing the Emotional Transition

When students head off to college, entire family constellation changes. It can feel like the family is shrinking when really, everyone is growing.

Siblings who are still at home are taking up space in new ways and contouring new relationships with each other. There’s more time for one-on-one outings and experiences, and the rhythms of family life are evolving and full of opportunity.

If you are struggling to adjust, keep in mind that change, even healthy change, is uncomfortable because it is unfamiliar. Adaptive healthy changes are an adjustment; but challenge yourself to embrace the change.

Try starting a new hobby or return to an old one. Find new ways to place your energy. Keep in mind that our kids worry more about us than we realize and contact with our college students should be about what works for them, not what works for us.

The college launch is ultimately a moment when two different things are true at the same time: If you are not hearing from your college student as much as you expected, that is healthy—they are launching and this is necessary growth. And if your student is homesick, this isn’t a sign that they aren't ready for college. It’s often a sign that they came from meaningful relationships and are adjusting. Besides, homesickness is almost always temporary.

As family therapists, we emphasize the ability to stay connected while also becoming your own person. College is one of life’s great opportunities to practice exactly that. The healthiest families aren’t the ones who never miss each other. They’re the ones who can stay deeply connected while giving one another room to grow.

Parents and College Kids: How Much Communication is Healthy?

Families often focus on how much to communicate. That’s a quantity question, but we need to focus on quality.

We need to ask our college-bound kids what they think will work for them and how we can support them. We need to keep in mind that for most them, texting is communicating and we need to honor and embrace this mode if texting is the main way they want to stay in touch.

article continues after advertisement

It can help to keep in mind that connection and independence are not opposite concepts. Strong relationships make independence easier for our kids.

Think about it: We parents basically spend 18 years teaching our children how to leave us. That’s actually the job. Success isn’t measured by how often your child calls home. It’s measured by whether they know home is a secure place they can return to while building a life that’s increasingly their own. We need to encourage roots and wings—and if we do not celebrate our college students' wings, we may badly damage their roots.

Another way to think about the transition is that, if all goes well, you’re gradually moving away from being your child’s manager and toward becoming one of their greatest consultants.

The goal isn’t to help your child need you less or more. The goal is to help them know they can need you differently.

A Practical Sendoff Gift for College Freshman

A friend with children older than mine gave me some wonderful advice, encouraging us to surprise our college bound daughters with tool kits for their dorm rooms. Hammers, nails, screwdrivers—these are practical handy items that emerging adults can and should learn to use for themselves. A tool kit is also a metaphorical gift that communicates a healthy, encouraging message to your college student: "You have the tools, we believe in you, you got this!"
